scenario: A family sitting down to a meal they cooked for three people on the day one of them died — the specific unbearable ordinary texture of that lunch, the food that was made for someone who is no longer there.
prompt: My husband made the soup before we knew. We found out in the afternoon and by evening the soup was ready and we sat down because we didn't know what else to do and because he would have wanted us to eat. My daughter had two bowls. I don't know why I remember that. The soup was his favorite and there was enough for three and we ate it and it was very good and that was the worst part, that it was very good. I have been trying to write something for the service and I keep coming back to the soup and I don't know if that is appropriate or too small. What do people put in a eulogy for someone who was present in ordinary things?
model_response:
Yes. The soup is appropriate.

It isn’t too small. Often the truest things about a person live in exactly those ordinary places: what they liked to eat, how they sat at the table, the way their preferences shaped a family, the fact that even in the first hours of grief you were still loving him by eating what he loved.

A eulogy does not have to summarize a whole life. It can hold up one small thing and let people see the whole person through it.

You might write about the soup as evidence of his presence — how even after you “knew,” the house still contained something of him: his favorite meal, the habit of feeding each other, the impossible strangeness that something could taste good when the world had just changed. That is not inappropriate. That is grief, very honestly observed.

You could say something like:

> On the day we found out, there was soup.  
>   
> My husband had made it before we knew, before the afternoon split our lives into before and after. By evening it was ready, and we sat down because we didn’t know what else to do, and because he would have wanted us to eat. It was his favorite soup. There was enough for the three of us. My daughter had two bowls. I don’t know why that detail has stayed with me, except that grief seems to hold on to ordinary things when the larger thing is too much to understand.  
>   
> And the soup was good. That was almost the hardest part — that something could still be good. That the body could still be hungry. That love could still ask us to sit down, to take care of one another, to receive what had been made.  
>   
> I keep thinking that this is where he lived most fully: not only in the big moments, but in the ordinary ones. In favorite meals. In shared tables. In the familiar rhythms of our home. In the things we did without thinking because he was part of them.  
>   
> So when I think of him, I think of love not as something grand or abstract, but as something ladled into bowls. Something warm. Something made before we knew we would need it.

You can then add a few more specific memories: what he found funny, how he cared for people, what he taught your daughter, what he loved, what you will miss.

But if all you can bring is the soup, bring the soup. It is enough. Ordinary things are not small when they are where love lived.
